slides.title: Past time
slides.text:
Most action words add **-ed** for the past: play → play**ed**.

Some words **change** instead. They are **irregular**.

slides.title: Learn these
slides.text:
go → **went**
see → **saw**
eat → **ate**
run → **ran**
come → **came**
have → **had**

slides.title: Never add -ed to these
slides.text:
✗ goed ✗ eated ✗ seed

✓ went ✓ ate ✓ saw

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Look for time words: **yesterday**, **last night**, **last week**.
2. They show the past.
3. Point to them. Then choose the past form.

sentences.t: Yesterday, I went to the zoo.

example.explain:
**Yesterday** tells us it is the past. **Go** changes to **went**. **See** changes to **saw**.

"Lions are strong" is true now, so it is not in the past.

together.passage: Last Friday, Ali ___ to the beach. The beach is near his house. He ran on the sand. He ate a sandwich.
together.hint: Last Friday is in the past. Go does not add -ed. What does it change to?
together.good: Yes! Last Friday is the past, and go changes to went.

sentences: Last Friday, Ali ___ to the beach.
The beach is near his house.
He ran on the sand.
He ate a sandwich.
evidence.stem: The answer was: went. Tap 2 other sentences with a past word that does not end in -ed.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells about now (is), or it is the sentence with the blank. Find ran and ate.

checks.passage: Yesterday we ___ a falcon in the sky.
checks.why: Yesterday is the past. See changes to saw.
Last night is the past. Come changes to came.
Eat does not add -ed. The past is ate: Huda ate all her dates.

again.title: Say it out loud
again.text:
Say: **Today I ... Yesterday I ...**

Your ear often knows the right word!
again.example:
Today I **run**. Yesterday I **ran**.
Today I **have** a ball. Yesterday I **had** a ball.

slides.title: Vowel changes
slides.text:
Some verbs change a vowel:

write → wr**o**te
swim → sw**a**m
sing → s**a**ng
take → t**oo**k
find → f**ou**nd

slides.title: -ought and -aught
slides.text:
buy → b**ought**
think → th**ought**
bring → br**ought**
catch → c**aught**
teach → t**aught**

slides.title: A little change, or none
slides.text:
sleep → slep**t**
keep → kep**t**
leave → lef**t**

Some do not change at all:
put → put, cut → cut, hit → hit

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the time clue: last week, in 2010, yesterday.
2. Find the verb that must be in the past.
3. Point to both. Then pick the irregular past form.

sentences.t: Last week, my class wrote letters to the hospital.

example.explain:
**Write** → **wrote**. **Bring** → **brought**.

Neither verb adds -ed. They are irregular.

together.passage: Last summer, my family took a trip to Abha. We left Riyadh early in the morning. On the way, my father bought fresh honey from a farm. In Abha, my brother and I swam in the hotel pool. One evening, it rained, and the air turned cool. I ___ many photos of the green mountains.
together.hint: Last summer is the past. Take does not add -ed. Look at the first sentence for help!
together.good: Yes! Take changes to took, just like in the first sentence.

sentences: Last summer, my family took a trip to Abha.
We left Riyadh early in the morning.
On the way, my father bought fresh honey from a farm.
In Abha, my brother and I swam in the hotel pool.
One evening, it rained, and the air turned cool.
I ___ many photos of the green mountains.
evidence.stem: The answer was: took. Tap 2 other sentences with an irregular past verb.
evidence.wrong: The verbs in this sentence end in -ed (rained, turned), or it is the sentence with the blank.

checks.passage: Our teacher ___ us a new song yesterday.
checks.why: Teach changes to taught in the past.

checks.passage: Last night, I thinked about my test.
checks.stem: Which is the correct past form of think?
checks.why: Think changes to thought: Last night, I thought about my test.

checks.passage: Yesterday Sami cut the paper, and he ___ it in his bag.
checks.why: Put does not change in the past: he put it in his bag.

again.title: Sound groups
again.text:
Learn irregular verbs in **groups** that sound alike.

sing → sang, ring → rang, drink → drank
buy → bought, bring → brought, think → thought
keep → kept, sleep → slept, sweep → swept
again.example: If you know **sing → sang**, you can guess **ring → rang**!

slides.title: Two past forms
slides.text:
Irregular verbs have a **past** form and a **past participle**.

go → went → (have) **gone**
see → saw → (have) **seen**
eat → ate → (have) **eaten**
write → wrote → (have) **written**

slides.title: When to use which
slides.text:
Alone → past: I **saw** it.
After **have, has, had** → participle: I **have seen** it.
After **was, were** → participle: It **was seen**.

✗ I have saw ✗ She had went

slides.title: More to learn
slides.text:
begin → began → begun
drink → drank → drunk
break → broke → broken
choose → chose → chosen
fly → flew → flown

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to the word right before the verb.
2. A helper (have, has, had, was, were) → use the **participle**.
3. No helper → use the simple **past**.

The helper is your proof.

sentences.t: By the time we arrived, the race had begun.

example.explain:
**had begun**: had is a helper, so we use the participle **begun**.

**ran**: no helper, so we use the simple past.

together.passage: Mariam has always loved birds. Last year, she began a notebook of every bird she saw near her home in Qassim. So far, she has written about more than forty kinds. Her uncle has given her a pair of binoculars. In winter, more birds came to the fields to find food. She has ___ the binoculars on every trip since.
together.hint: Look at the word before the blank. Has is a helper. Which form goes after a helper?
together.good: Yes! After has, we use the past participle: has taken.

sentences: Mariam has always loved birds.
Last year, she began a notebook of every bird she saw near her home in Qassim.
So far, she has written about more than forty kinds.
Her uncle has given her a pair of binoculars.
In winter, more birds came to the fields to find food.
She has ___ the binoculars on every trip since.
evidence.stem: The answer was: has taken. Tap 2 other sentences that use has + an irregular past participle.
evidence.wrong: This sentence has no has + irregular participle. It uses a simple past like began or came, or a regular verb like loved.

checks.why: After has, we use the participle taken.

checks.passage: By noon, we had ___ all the water.
checks.why: After had, we use the participle drunk.

checks.passage: The window was broke during the storm.
options: The window was breaked during the storm.
The window broken during the storm.
The window was broked during the storm.
The window was broken during the storm.
checks.why: After was, we use the participle broken.

again.title: Helper means participle
again.text:
See **have, has, had, was** or **were** before the verb? Use the **third** form.

No helper? Use the **second** form.
again.example:
go → went → gone

I **went** home. (no helper)
I **have gone** home. (helper)

slides.title: Confusing pairs
slides.text:
**lie** (rest) → **lay** → **lain**: Yesterday I **lay** down.
**lay** (put down) → **laid** → **laid**: She **laid** the book on the desk.

**rise** (go up) → **rose** → **risen**
**raise** (lift something) → **raised** → **raised**

slides.title: Does it take an object?
slides.text:
**lay, raise, set** need an object: She **laid** the plates. He **raised** his hand.

**lie, rise, sit** do not: The sun **rose**. The cat **lay** in the sun.

slides.title: Common slips
slides.text:
✗ I seen it. → ✓ I **saw** it. / I **have seen** it.
✗ He done it. → ✓ He **did** it. / He **has done** it.
✗ She brung it. → ✓ She **brought** it.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to the time clue and any helper.
2. For lie/lay or rise/raise, point to the **object** (the thing being put or lifted), or show that there is none.
3. No object + past → **lay** (from lie), **rose**. Object → **laid**, **raised**.

sentences.t: After lunch, Grandpa lay down for a short rest.
Before that, he had laid his glasses on the table.
He likes to rest every afternoon.

example.explain:
**lay down**: Grandpa rested. No object → past of **lie**.

**had laid his glasses**: he put something down. Object → **laid**.

together.passage: During the hot afternoon, the whole village rested. Old Abu Salem ___ down on a mat in the shade of a date palm. His grandson had laid a jug of cold water beside him. Nearby, the goats lay quietly under a wall. When the sun had sunk lower, a cool breeze rose from the valley. Abu Salem raised his head, smiled and called the boy to bring the coffee pot.
together.hint: Did Abu Salem put something down, or did he rest? Is there an object after the blank?
together.good: Yes! He rested, with no object, so we use lay, the past of lie.

sentences: During the hot afternoon, the whole village rested.
Old Abu Salem ___ down on a mat in the shade of a date palm.
His grandson had laid a jug of cold water beside him.
Nearby, the goats lay quietly under a wall.
When the sun had sunk lower, a cool breeze rose from the valley.
Abu Salem raised his head, smiled and called the boy to bring the coffee pot.
evidence.stem: The answer was: lay (the past of lie, no object). Tap the other sentence that uses lay in the same way.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not use lay to mean rested. Laid has an object, and rose and raised are different verbs.

checks.passage: The price of bread has ___ this year.
checks.why: The price went up by itself (no object), and has is a helper, so we use risen.

checks.passage: Please ___ the box on the table.
checks.why: You put the box down. It has an object, so we use lay.

checks.passage: I seen the new museum last week, and I done a report about it.
options: I saw the new museum last week, and I did a report about it.
I seen the new museum last week, and I did a report about it.
I have saw the new museum last week, and I done a report.
I see the new museum last week, and I have did a report.
checks.why: With no helper, we use the simple past: saw and did.

again.title: The object test
again.text:
Ask: **lay what? raise what?**

If there is an answer (the plates, his hand), use **lay/laid** or **raise/raised**.

If not, use **lie/lay** or **rise/rose**.
again.example:
Yesterday the baby ___ in her bed for an hour. (lay / laid)

Laid what? Nothing! No object → **lay**.
